title: USACE teams conduct FEMA-assigned Hurricane Ian infrastructure assessments
description: Baltimore District Structural Engineer Kent Morey and U.S. Army Corps of Engineers teams conduct FEMA-assigned infrastructure assessments on Sanibel Island, Florida, Nov. 8. The USACE inspectors are working in coordination with Florida state and county officials to assess the structures in accordance with Applied Technology Council safety evaluation standards. In addition to the infrastructure assessments, USACE is actively supporting FEMA Hurricane Ian recovery efforts in other areas, to include temporary blue roof installations, temporary housing and debris technical assistance.

transcript.text: My name is Kent Mori. I'm with the Baltimore District. I'm a structural engineer that works in our
construction division. I'm down here responding to Hurricane Ian. We're doing infrastructure
assessments. There's two types of infrastructure assessments that we do. One is a rapid assessment.
Most of those have been done already here on Sanibel Island. We're working on a detailed
assessment today because the rapid assessment recommended a detailed assessment is done for
structural reasons. There's certain aspects to a building or parts of a building that are there
for aesthetic purposes. What we're trying to decipher is what actual structural issues are.
That may, you may see that some partition walls or stucco or siding and roofing may be missing
or compromised, but that doesn't necessarily mean the structure behind it is damaged as well.
We also look at any geotechnical issues that may be occurring, such as scour around some of the
pilings, missing footings, you know, cracked or damaged foundation walls. We're looking for the
structure's leaning. If the structure has been racking, if there's any disconnection between walls and
floors, if there's any disconnection between the footing and the superstructure, that is the walls.
These are some of the typical problems that we might find out here. Every homeowner or our
structure owner is going to get this assessment or have access to this assessment. They may see a
lot of damage at their house and not really recognize whether it's structural or not. It could help
them make decisions on whether they want to renovate their house or tear it down. These people have
been dealt a serious blow and if I can help them in any way, it's extremely gratifying, especially
when you talk to some of these homeowners. They're very, very grateful that you're here. Nobody's
chased us away. Nobody's asked us to not look at their structure. They're very welcoming. They
appreciate the effort that we do. And so for me personally, that's very gratifying to have somebody
clearly recognize that you're helping them and they appreciate your efforts.
